name: Nellaiappar Temple, Tirunelveli
deity: Shiva as Nellaiappar, guardian of the paddy, with the Goddess Kanthimathi
period: Pandya and Chola origins; the great halls and musical pillars added under the Nayaks
dynasty: Pandya and Chola origins, Nayaka additions
summary: In the old town of Tirunelveli on the Tamiraparani river, twin temples of Shiva as Nellaiappar and the Goddess Kanthimathi stand joined by a chain of halls — a great Shaiva shrine famous for stone pillars that ring with music and for the copper hall where Shiva is said to have danced.

sections.history: The Nellaiappar temple stands at Tirunelveli, an ancient town on the banks of the Tamiraparani in the far south of Tamil Nadu. It is a Paadal Petra Sthalam, sung in the Tevaram hymns of the Nayanmar saints, with origins under the Pandyas and Cholas and its great mandapas and towers raised in the later centuries under Nayaka rule. The temple is really two — the shrine of Shiva as Nellaiappar and, beside it, the shrine of the Goddess Kanthimathi — joined into a single vast complex, at the devotional heart of a town whose name itself recalls the lord who guarded a devotee's paddy.
sections.architecture: The complex is entered through tall gopurams and unfolds through pillared halls of the mature Dravidian manner, the twin temples of Nellaiappar and Kanthimathi linked by the Sangili Mandapam, the 'chain hall'. Its most celebrated feature is the group of musical pillars — clusters of slender stone columns, carved from single blocks, that sound different musical notes when struck. Tirunelveli is honoured as the Tamira Sabhai, the copper hall, one of the five sabhas where Shiva is said to have danced his cosmic dance, and the temple holds a golden-lily tank and richly sculptured mandapas among the finest of the Nayaka age.
sections.legends: The name Nellaiappar — the lord of the nel, the paddy — comes from a beloved legend: a devotee had spread his harvested paddy to dry when the rains threatened, and the lord held back the downpour, sheltering the grain, so that he became known as the guardian of the paddy, Venuvananathar of the bamboo forest. The Goddess Kanthimathi shines beside him as the light of the shrine. Tirunelveli's place among the five dance-halls, as the copper sabha, sets its worship within the great tradition of Shiva Nataraja, whose foremost hall is the golden one at Chidambaram.
sections.festivals: The temple's year is marked by the Aadi and the Brahmotsavam festivals, the float festival on the golden-lily tank, and the Arudra Darshan sacred to Shiva as the dancer. The car festival draws great crowds through the streets of the old town. Music has a natural home here, in the temple of the singing pillars, and festival days fill the long halls with lamps, song and pilgrims.
sections.experience: Nellaiappar rewards the visitor who lingers among its halls: the ring of the musical pillars, the sculptured mandapas, the twin sanctums of god and goddess joined by the chain hall, and the river town around it. Tirunelveli sits in the deep south of Tamil Nadu, an easy journey from Thiruchendur on the coast and from the land's end at Kanyakumari, and joins them into a single pilgrimage of the far south.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan sessions and a long midday closure; festival days are busiest. Confirm current timings before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Men are traditionally asked to remove the upper garment before entering the sanctum, as at many southern shrines; follow the posted rules.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted, especially in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Tirunelveli is a major town in the deep south of Tamil Nadu, well connected by road and rail; it lies about 60 km from Thiruchendur and within easy reach of Kanyakumari and the far south.
